paragraphs: This paper studies representative democracy as a mathematical decision-making system. Its starting point is a setting in which voters may have noisy or limited information. When average voter competence falls below one half, direct voting fails in the setting described by the authors. Choosing representatives can potentially improve decisions in these circumstances.

The authors introduce a model for asking which features of a representative system maximize its decision-making capability. A central design choice is how many representatives to use. The analysis connects this choice to the cost of voting, making the cost model part of the mathematical question rather than treating representation as a purely qualitative alternative.

Under conditions described as general and natural, the optimal number of representatives has linear scaling when voting cost is fixed and logarithmic scaling when cost is polynomial. These are conditional conclusions within the proposed model. Their significance is that changing the cost assumption changes the form of the optimal representative count, giving a precise way to study institutional design.
neurips-2018-a-mathematical-model-for-op.tldr: A mathematical model links the optimal number of representatives to voting costs under stated conditions.

paragraphs: The paper considers clustering when a dataset is divided across several sites. It studies the familiar k-means and k-median objectives while allowing a small portion of the observations to be labeled as outliers and discarded. The challenge is to form useful clusters and identify outliers across the full distributed dataset.

The proposed approach constructs a compact summary of the original data. This summary is the basis for an algorithm designed to use both computation time and communication efficiently. The method also has approximation guarantees, connecting its practical resource savings to a theoretical account of the quality of the clustering solution it produces.

The authors report that the algorithm can effectively identify global outliers and describe it, to their knowledge, as the first practical distributed method for this problem with theoretical guarantees. Experiments on real and synthetic data show advantages over all tested baselines on almost all measured criteria. That evidence supports the combination of compact summaries, distributed operation, and explicit outlier handling in the evaluated settings.
neurips-2018-a-practical-algorithm-for-d.tldr: Compact data summaries enable efficient distributed clustering with outlier detection and theoretical approximation guarantees.

paragraphs: The paper develops a faster version of Stein variational gradient descent, or SVGD, a method for approximating probability distributions. SVGD improves an approximation by reducing its Kullback–Leibler divergence from a target distribution. Its updates take the form of gradient descent over functions in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space.

The proposed method adds second-order information to those updates. In ordinary optimization, such information describes curvature and can help determine how an update should respond to the shape of an objective. Here, the authors use it to approximate a Newton-style iteration in function space, extending the machinery used by the original SVGD algorithm.

Second-order information also informs the choice of kernel, another component of the approximation procedure. The authors show how it can lead to more effective kernel choices and report substantial computational gains over SVGD across multiple test cases. The contribution therefore has two connected parts: a curvature-informed update and a way to use the same information when choosing the kernel that supports it.
neurips-2018-a-stein-variational-newton-.tldr: A Newton-style extension of SVGD uses second-order information for updates and kernel selection, with computational gains in multiple tests.

paragraphs: A classifier can perform well on ordinary inputs yet make confident errors after small adversarial changes. This paper examines that mismatch through generalization: how much training data is needed to perform reliably on new examples. It asks whether learning robustness can demand more information than learning accurate predictions on unmodified inputs.

The authors prove that a substantial gap in data requirements can arise even in a simple, natural data model. The gap is information theoretic, so within that setting it does not depend on choosing a particular training algorithm or model family. A different learning procedure alone cannot remove the data requirement established by the result.

Experiments on widely used image classification datasets reveal a similar gap, complementing the theoretical analysis with empirical evidence. The authors suggest that greater sample complexity explains at least part of the difficulty of training robust classifiers. This is a proposed partial explanation, while the formal result establishes that increased data requirements can be an inherent feature of robust learning in the analyzed model.
neurips-2018-adversarially-robust-genera.tldr: Robust learning can inherently require substantially more data than standard learning, with a similar gap observed in image experiments.

paragraphs: Evaluating a generative model involves at least two questions: whether its samples are good and whether they represent the variety in the target distribution. A single score can respond to both issues without revealing which one causes a poor result. The paper identifies this ambiguity in commonly used evaluation measures, including FID.

The authors define precision and recall for probability distributions to separate these aspects of comparison. Their definition gives two dimensions of assessment and leads to an efficient evaluation algorithm. They also connect it mathematically to total variation and relate it to established measures such as Inception Score and FID.

An empirical study of several GAN and variational autoencoder variants tests the usefulness of this separation. Across an extensive collection of experiments, the proposed measure distinguishes generated-sample quality from coverage of the target distribution. The practical contribution is a more informative diagnosis: comparisons can expose different failure patterns that would otherwise be compressed into one number, making the nature of a model's performance easier to interpret.
neurips-2018-assessing-generative-models.tldr: Distributional precision and recall separate the quality of generated samples from coverage of the target distribution.

paragraphs: Dual Swap Disentangling learns representations whose separate parts capture interpretable attributes. It uses both labeled and unlabeled examples, with limited supervision indicating that two samples share an attribute such as color. This paired information supplies guidance without requiring complete annotations for an entire group of samples.

The model uses a dual autoencoder structure. For a labeled pair, it encodes both inputs, exchanges the encoding portions assigned to their shared attribute, and decodes the resulting combinations to reconstruct the originals. Because the attribute is shared, this reconstruction objective encourages its encoding to be transferable between the paired examples.

For unlabeled pairs, the model performs the encoding, swapping, and decoding process twice, requiring the final outputs to approximate the initial inputs. These exchanges encourage selected encoding dimensions to behave as portable modules, guided by the labeled pairs. The authors report state-of-the-art disentangling performance across image datasets from varied domains. The findings support using reconstruction through repeated swaps to extend a small amount of attribute supervision to unlabeled data.
neurips-2018-dual-swap-disentangling-c21.tldr: Dual Swap Disentangling uses paired attribute labels and repeated encoding swaps to learn disentangled representations from labeled and unlabeled images.

paragraphs: Structured prediction tasks often have evaluation measures that reflect the actual errors users care about, such as edit distance or n-gram mismatch. Training commonly uses a different objective, such as cross-entropy, because directly computing gradients for these structured losses can become intractable. The paper addresses this computational obstacle to aligning training with evaluation.

The authors develop efficient gradient algorithms for two broad loss families, called rational and tropical losses. These include edit-distance and n-gram losses as well as other sequence-similarity measures used in natural language processing and computational biology. The contribution therefore covers a collection of related objectives rather than a single specialized loss.

The algorithms organize computation using weighted automata and graph operations over suitable semirings. These mathematical structures provide a way to carry out the gradient calculations efficiently. As a result, models including neural networks can be trained with complex structured losses from the supported families. The stated advance is computational feasibility for these objectives, enabling training to use losses that would be difficult to handle through a naive implementation.
neurips-2018-efficient-gradient-computat.tldr: Efficient gradient algorithms make broad families of structured losses, including edit-distance and n-gram losses, usable for model training.

paragraphs: Ephemeral Value Adjustments, or EVA, gives a deep reinforcement learning agent a way to adapt rapidly using experiences already stored in its replay buffer. The method focuses on value estimates, which assess the usefulness of states or decisions. It combines a neural network's prediction with an additional estimate obtained from remembered experience.

For the current state, EVA retrieves nearby experience tuples from the replay buffer. It then applies prioritized sweeping over those experiences to estimate values and uses the result to shift the value predicted by the network. This makes local stored experience part of the agent's value computation rather than relying solely on the network prediction.

The approach brings together three memory-related ideas: storage in slots, retrieval based on content, and planning with retrieved memories. Their combination connects the current situation to relevant past experience and uses that experience to adjust estimates online. The authors report good performance on a demonstration task and Atari games, supporting this combination as a workable mechanism for incorporating memory-based adaptation into deep reinforcement learning.
neurips-2018-fast-deep-reinforcement-lea.tldr: EVA adjusts neural value predictions using planning over nearby replay-buffer experiences to support rapid adaptation.

paragraphs: Predicting physical behavior requires representing both an object's structure and its interactions with other objects. This paper proposes a hierarchical particle representation that accommodates a broad range of three-dimensional objects. The representation covers rigid objects with arbitrary geometry as well as deformable materials, allowing different kinds of physical structure to share a common framework.

The authors pair this representation with the Hierarchical Relation Network, or HRN. It uses graph convolution across the hierarchy to learn physical dynamics and is differentiable from end to end. The representation and network are connected design choices: the hierarchy organizes the objects, while the network learns relationships within that organization to predict their behavior.

Compared with other neural network baselines, HRN handles complex collisions and nonrigid deformation accurately in the reported results. It also produces plausible long-term predictions in new settings and scales to large scene configurations. These findings support the architecture's potential as a foundation for future physics predictors in vision, robotics, and cognitive science; the proposed applications are possibilities motivated by the demonstrated predictive behavior.
neurips-2018-flexible-neural-representat.tldr: A hierarchical particle representation and graph network predict collisions and deformations across varied three-dimensional objects and scenes.

paragraphs: Low-rank matrix recovery reconstructs a matrix from linear measurements. One route to proving exact recovery uses restricted isometry, meaning the measurements approximately preserve relevant norms. This paper examines how strong that property must be to rule out spurious local minima: locally attractive solutions that do not give the desired recovery.

The authors show that moderate restricted isometry does not suffice. Their counterexample construction makes any chosen x a spurious local minimum of some rank-one recovery instance satisfying restricted isometry. This claim concerns a corresponding constructed instance for each x. It demonstrates that merely having norm-preserving measurements does not by itself establish a favorable optimization landscape.

In one counterexample with restricted isometry constant one half, randomly initialized stochastic gradient descent fails in 12 percent of runs. Although SGD often avoids or escapes spurious minima, this experiment shows they can sometimes defeat it. The authors conclude that landscape guarantees based only on norm preservation apply to a narrow range of nearly isotropic instances, and suggest that exact recovery guarantees will likely need proofs excluding spurious minima.
neurips-2018-how-much-restricted-isometr.tldr: Counterexamples show that moderate restricted isometry does not eliminate spurious local minima in nonconvex matrix recovery.

paragraphs: The paper approaches adversarial robustness through the gap between human and neural-network perception. Small changes can alter a network's prediction while remaining imperceptible to people. The authors seek a robust classifier whose adversarial examples resemble ordinary data from the attack's target class, making successful attacks visually meaningful.

They formulate training in a GAN-style framework. An attack on the classifier acts as a generator, while a critic learns to distinguish ordinary images from adversarial ones. The classifier's objective includes making its adversarial examples confuse that critic. This connects classifier training to whether the resulting attacks look like regular examples of their intended target.

The method also introduces adversarial cycle consistency: applying the adversarial mapping again to an adversarial example should produce something close to the original input. This constraint is intended to stabilize the mapping. In the reported experiments, the defense exceeds the robustness of networks trained with adversarial training. Human-annotation experiments additionally find the adversarial examples visually confusing, supporting the paper's aim of bringing network confusion closer to human confusion.
neurips-2018-improved-network-robustness.tldr: An adversary critic and cycle-consistency constraint train classifiers whose successful adversarial examples are more visually confusing to people.

paragraphs: This paper studies learning a control policy for a linear dynamical system whose parameters are unknown. The controller aims to maximize a quadratic reward, so its decisions are evaluated through a particular mathematical measure of performance. Observed data provide information about the system, but uncertainty about its parameters remains part of the problem.

The proposed method optimizes reward averaged over the posterior distribution of those unknown parameters. In other words, the objective accounts for a distribution of possible systems supported by the data. The algorithm uses sequential convex programming, organizing the optimization as a sequence of convex programs, and has reliable local convergence and robust stability guarantees.

The authors demonstrate the approach in numerical simulations and by stabilizing a real inverted pendulum. Both settings show strong performance and robustness in their reported results. The combination matters because the method addresses uncertainty in the control objective while also supplying stability guarantees. Its convergence claim is local, and the demonstrations provide practical evidence for the approach in the systems that were studied.
neurips-2018-learning-convex-bounds-for-.tldr: Sequential convex programming learns linear-quadratic controllers that account for parameter uncertainty and provide local convergence and robust stability guarantees.

paragraphs: Cutting-plane methods solve optimization problems by accumulating constraints that guide subsequent steps. For the original simplicial method applied to composite convex and submodular objectives, the subproblems grow with every iteration, and a convergence rate was not known. This paper develops limited-memory variants that prevent this continuing growth.

The proposed L-KM method retains at most n plus one constraints for an n-dimensional problem, independent of how many iterations it runs. The authors prove convergence when the convex component of the objective is strongly convex. When that component is also smooth, they establish linear convergence, giving a rate guarantee under these additional conditions.

The analysis connects the original problem to a dual optimization problem over a submodular base polytope. A limited-memory, fully corrective Frank-Wolfe method with approximate correction solves this dual problem. The authors show that it and L-KM generate the same iterate sequence, transferring the convergence and memory guarantees between them. Their Frank-Wolfe results also extend to general polytopes, giving that part of the analysis relevance beyond the original composite objective.
neurips-2018-limited-memory-kelley-s-met.tldr: Limited-memory cutting-plane and Frank-Wolfe methods retain convergence guarantees, including linear convergence under smoothness and strong convexity.

paragraphs: Multiset prediction maps an input to a collection of items in which order is unspecified and repeated items are allowed. Both features matter: the predictor must handle which items occur and their multiplicities without assuming a known target ordering. This makes the task different from ordinary classification, ranking, and sequence generation.

The authors propose a loss function by viewing multiset prediction as sequential decision making. This perspective provides a way to organize the prediction process even though the target collection has no known order. The central contribution is the training objective, designed around the structure of a multiset rather than simply adopting an objective from a neighboring prediction task.

The loss is evaluated on synthetic and real dataset families with varying difficulty. Comparisons include objectives based on reinforcement learning, sequence prediction, and aggregated distribution matching. The experiments favor the proposed loss over these alternatives. These findings support treating unordered collections with repetitions as a distinct learning problem and designing the loss accordingly, with the reported effectiveness established through the evaluated datasets and comparisons.
neurips-2018-loss-functions-for-multiset.tldr: A sequential-decision-based loss improves multiset prediction in experiments involving unordered outputs with repeated items.

paragraphs: Structured prediction addresses supervised learning problems whose outputs have meaningful internal structure. Traditional formulations often use finite output spaces, even when those spaces are enormous. This paper extends the perspective to continuous outputs, concentrating on regression problems whose predictions lie on a manifold, a space with its own geometric structure.

The authors characterize a class of problems for which their structured prediction approach is statistically consistent. This gives a theoretical connection between learning from data and the desired prediction behavior as data increase, within the identified class. They also study geometric optimization as a way to compute the estimator while respecting the structure of its output space.

Experiments on simulated and real data provide promising evidence for the approach. The contribution brings together a continuous structured-output formulation, a consistency analysis, and a computational treatment using geometry. That combination matters because a structured prediction method needs both a statistical justification and a way to obtain predictions. The consistency claim applies to the characterized problems, while the experiments illustrate its practical promise.
neurips-2018-manifold-structured-predict.tldr: Structured prediction is extended to manifold-valued regression with consistency results for a characterized problem class and geometric optimization methods.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks offer a flexible, data-driven approach to classification on graphs. This paper asks how well that flexibility translates into accuracy and how much of the resulting performance comes from the architecture itself versus learning through backpropagation. These questions motivate a theoretical analysis of graph partitioning.

The authors develop a mean-field theory for a minimal GNN architecture on this problem. Choosing a minimal architecture makes a specific graph-learning system the object of analysis. The aim is to gain insight into its behavior and the sources of its performance, addressing questions that would be harder to disentangle from empirical accuracy alone.

The theoretical analysis agrees well with numerical experiments. This agreement supports the theory as a useful description of the studied architecture in graph partitioning. It provides an analytical foothold for examining why a GNN performs as it does. The stated finding is the match between theory and experiments; the abstract frames architecture versus backpropagation as a motivating question without assigning a universal share of performance to either.
neurips-2018-mean-field-theory-of-graph-.tldr: A mean-field analysis of a minimal graph neural network closely matches numerical experiments on graph partitioning.

paragraphs: The paper develops a way to measure differences between nonlinear dynamical systems. Here, the objects being compared are systems that evolve over time, making their dynamic structure central to the comparison. Defining a useful metric for such structured objects is the broader pattern-recognition and machine-learning problem motivating the work.

The proposed metric uses Perron-Frobenius operators represented in reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces. This operator-based formulation supplies a common mathematical framework for the comparison. It includes established dynamical-system metrics as special cases, specifically ones based on principal angles between appropriately selected subspaces. Thus, the construction generalizes existing geometric comparisons rather than standing apart from them.

The authors also describe how to estimate the metric from finite data, connecting the mathematical definition to observations available in practice. They illustrate its behavior using rotation dynamics within a unit disk in the complex plane and evaluate it on real time-series data. These studies provide examples of the metric in use, while the main contribution is a general comparison framework with both connections to prior metrics and a data-based estimation procedure.
neurips-2018-metric-on-nonlinear-dynamic.tldr: An operator-based metric compares nonlinear dynamical systems, generalizes existing geometric metrics, and can be estimated from finite data.

paragraphs: Natural images contain similar structures at different locations, and classical restoration methods have used this self-similarity effectively. The paper develops a non-local recurrent network, NLRN, to incorporate that property into a trainable deep model. Its non-local module captures correlations between deep features at an image location and those in its neighborhood.

The recurrent structure reuses parameters and carries feature correlations between adjacent recurrent states. This propagation improves robustness when image degradation makes correlation estimates inaccurate. The authors also find it essential to confine the neighborhood used for correlation computation on degraded images, rather than using the whole image as in existing practice.

The module can be integrated into deep networks for end-to-end training, so similarity estimation becomes part of the learned restoration process. Experiments cover image denoising and super-resolution. The reported results exceed those of state-of-the-art methods while using many fewer parameters. Together, the findings support recurrent non-local operations and correlation propagation as an effective way to exploit image self-similarity under degradation in the evaluated restoration tasks.
neurips-2018-non-local-recurrent-network.tldr: NLRN propagates learned image-feature correlations through recurrent states to improve restoration with fewer parameters.

paragraphs: Convolution works naturally on images because their grid gives nearby values a consistent spatial arrangement. Point clouds have irregular locations and no inherent ordering. Applying ordinary convolution directly to point features can therefore lose shape information and make the result depend on an arbitrary ordering of the points.

PointCNN addresses this problem by learning an X-transformation from the input points. The transformation both weights their associated features and rearranges them into a learned, potentially canonical order. Standard convolution-style multiplication and summation then operate on the transformed features. This makes the learned transformation the bridge between irregular point data and the familiar convolution operation.

The framework generalizes convolutional feature learning to point clouds while explicitly addressing their geometry and ordering difficulties. The ordering is described as potentially canonical, so the proposal should not be read as an unconditional guarantee of a unique ordering. Across multiple challenging benchmark datasets and tasks, the authors report performance matching or exceeding state-of-the-art methods, supporting the practical effectiveness of the transformation-based approach in those evaluations.
neurips-2018-pointcnn-convolution-on-x-t.tldr: PointCNN learns to weight and reorder point features before convolution, enabling effective feature learning on irregular point clouds.

paragraphs: A Nash equilibrium can leave rational behavior unspecified in situations that its own strategies assign zero probability. Such situations can still arise when players make mistakes. Trembling-hand refinements address this weakness, including extensive-form perfect and quasi-perfect equilibria. Their practical use had been constrained by algorithms that could handle only very small games.

The paper introduces an exact polynomial-time algorithm for finding trembling-hand equilibria in zero-sum extensive-form games. These games represent sequences of decisions through a game tree. The contribution concerns computing a stronger equilibrium concept within this particular game setting, making strategies that account for otherwise unreached situations computationally accessible.

The authors report that the algorithm is numerically stable and several orders of magnitude faster than the best previous methods. It quickly solves instances whose game trees contain tens of thousands of nodes. This combination of exact computation and substantial practical speedup supports their claim that trembling-hand refinements become usable beyond toy examples. The result applies to the stated zero-sum extensive-form setting, where the algorithm's efficiency and exactness are established.
neurips-2018-practical-exact-algorithm-f.tldr: An exact polynomial-time algorithm makes trembling-hand equilibrium refinements practical for substantially larger zero-sum extensive-form games.

paragraphs: The paper seeks a low-dimensional linear subspace that represents a collection of data points while minimizing a loss applied to their distances from that subspace. When the loss is simply distance itself, the resulting objective is more resistant to outliers than truncated singular value decomposition. Computing the optimum is nevertheless NP-hard.

For fixed subspace dimension and fixed approximation tolerance, a solution within a factor of one plus that tolerance can be found in polynomial time. The authors bring this approximation problem into turnstile streaming and arbitrarily partitioned distributed settings. They give the first sublinear approximation algorithm for these models while retaining the time guarantees available in the offline case.

The algorithm relies entirely on oblivious dimensionality reduction, making that technique the foundation of the approach. The authors report that this substantially simplifies earlier methods, which did not apply in either of the studied data-access settings. The contribution combines robust subspace fitting with an algorithmic design suited to streaming or distributed data, preserving approximation guarantees under the stated fixed-dimension and fixed-tolerance conditions.
neurips-2018-robust-subspace-approximati.tldr: Oblivious dimensionality reduction enables guaranteed robust subspace approximation in streaming and distributed settings.

paragraphs: SEGA is an optimization method that learns about the gradient through random linear measurements called sketches. Instead of treating each measurement in isolation, it progressively builds a gradient estimate across iterations. This accumulated information supports variance reduction, allowing successive partial observations to contribute to the direction used for optimization.

Each iteration first updates the stored estimate through a sketch-and-project operation using the latest measurement. A random relaxation then produces an unbiased estimate of the true gradient, which supplies the next gradient step. The method also accommodates a non-separable proximal term, meaning that this part of the optimization problem can couple variables rather than splitting neatly across coordinates.

The authors provide a general convergence analysis and prove linear convergence for strongly convex objectives. When sketches select coordinates, SEGA can incorporate importance sampling, minibatches, and acceleration. In that setting, its rate matches the best-known coordinate-descent rate up to a small constant factor. The result connects efficient use of partial gradient information with guarantees and flexibility beyond standard subspace-descent methods.
neurips-2018-sega-variance-reduction-via.tldr: SEGA accumulates random gradient sketches into variance-reduced updates, with linear convergence for strongly convex objectives.

paragraphs: The paper asks whether samples come from a distribution that is uniform on some subset of a discrete domain. Neither the subset nor the size of the domain is assumed known. The alternative is that the distribution is at least epsilon away, in total variation distance, from every distribution of that form.

The authors construct a computationally efficient test that distinguishes these cases with probability at least two thirds. Its sample requirement is optimal up to constant factors, and a matching worst-case information-theoretic lower bound shows that the dependence cannot generally be improved beyond those factors. This addresses both how to test and how much data testing requires.

The required number of samples scales as the sum of 1/(epsilon^(4/3) ||p||_3) and 1/(epsilon^2 ||p||_2). Thus, the bound depends on the requested separation and on norms of the distribution itself. The result gives a sharp characterization for testing uniformity when its support is unspecified, tying an efficient procedure to a corresponding fundamental limit on sample use.
neurips-2018-sharp-bounds-for-generalize.tldr: An efficient test achieves sample-optimal generalized uniformity testing, with a matching worst-case lower bound.

paragraphs: The paper proposes a sampling method for Bayesian learning when the posterior distribution has multiple modes. Such a posterior contains several distinct regions of high probability, making exploration across those regions central to obtaining useful samples. The method also addresses noise introduced when computations use mini-batches of data.

The sampler simulates a noisy dynamical system that combines a continuously varying tempering variable with Nosé-Hoover thermostats. These components serve the combined aims of sampling a multimodal posterior and adapting to mini-batch noise. The authors state that the method can efficiently generate independent, identically distributed samples in the multimodal setting and adaptively neutralize the noise from mini-batching.

Synthetic datasets are used to study the approach's properties. Experiments on three real datasets, involving several types of neural networks, show performance gains over multiple strong Bayesian-learning baselines. The contribution is a sampling design that addresses multimodality and noisy computation together, with the reported experiments supporting its practical effectiveness across the evaluated neural-network settings.
neurips-2018-thermostat-assisted-continu.tldr: A continuously tempered Hamiltonian sampler uses thermostats to support multimodal Bayesian sampling while adapting to mini-batch noise.

paragraphs: Asynchronous momentum stochastic gradient descent combines two techniques used in distributed learning: momentum and updates that proceed asynchronously. Establishing convergence for complicated nonconvex applications is difficult. This paper studies streaming principal component analysis as a simpler but still nonconvex problem, using it to investigate how these two acceleration mechanisms interact.

The authors apply a diffusion approximation of stochastic optimization to derive the algorithm's asymptotic convergence rate for streaming PCA. Their analysis indicates a tradeoff: to obtain convergence and acceleration through asynchrony, momentum must be reduced relative to the synchronous momentum method. The two mechanisms therefore cannot simply be combined without accounting for their interaction in the analyzed setting.

Numerical experiments on streaming PCA and deep neural-network training support the findings. The formal convergence analysis concerns streaming PCA, while the neural-network experiments supply evidence relevant to a more complex application. The work provides a theoretical starting point for understanding asynchronous momentum in nonconvex optimization and a concrete reason to consider momentum and asynchrony jointly when assessing acceleration.
neurips-2018-towards-understanding-accel.tldr: Streaming-PCA analysis reveals a momentum–asynchrony tradeoff, supported by experiments on PCA and neural-network training.
